# AI Champions — Interview Questions and One-Sentence E7-Style Answers

Target: Meta E7 / senior principal TPM. Updated October 19, 2026.

These are rehearsal answers based on user-reported clarifications and the uploaded career document; they are not independent verification or a readiness verdict. Only question 1 is confirmed as asked in this visible thread. Questions 2–19 reproduce the nine interview prompts and nine follow-ups in Use Case_AI Champions_20261016.pdf; questions 20–36 are additional preparation prompts covering this thread’s established facts and gaps, not a reconstructed transcript of earlier sessions.

| # | Question | One-sentence answer |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Give me a 60–90-second executive overview of your AI Champions program: why it mattered, the strategic decisions you personally drove, and the outcomes you can substantiate. | I founded and led an adoption operating model that grew from 50 to 850 Champions by fiscal year-end, shifted toward high-value workflows as tools matured, and produced a two-team on-call pilot showing approximately 20% effort savings. |
| 2 | How did you found and lead an enterprise program without direct authority? | I connected executive sponsorship, local Champions, and six working groups through shared strategy, KPIs, enablement, and feedback mechanisms while preserving participating organizations’ ownership. |
| 3 | Did you manage the Champions? | I owned the program’s mechanisms and coordination without formally managing participating Champions or claiming their local achievements as my own. |
| 4 | When did feedback change your operating model? | I adapted central enablement, working groups, and local adoption support to address uneven maturity and information overload while retaining local ownership. |
| 5 | Why not centralize everything? | Central coordination could aggregate blockers and curate guidance, while local Champions understood the workflows and organizations where solutions needed to succeed. |
| 6 | How did your technical judgment turn adoption risks into program priorities? | I translated recurring context, access, connector, reliability, and governance friction into priorities for the specialist teams that owned implementation and approval. |
| 7 | Did you architect the AI platform? | I architected the adoption program and personally built the Happy Oncall prototype, while engineering and policy owners retained platform implementation and approval authority. |
| 8 | How did you report value without turning activity into ROI? | I separated reach, engagement, organizational coverage, and workflow adoption from productivity evidence, limiting the approximately 20% effort-savings claim to the two-team pilot. |
| 9 | What did the program actually achieve? | My self-reported results were growth from 50 to 850 members and coverage of every organization above 600 employees, alongside a two-team on-call pilot rather than demonstrated enterprise-wide productivity gains. |
| 10 | How did you manage the risk of launching an unfinished Impact Hub? | I advocated launching usable onboarding and directories while keeping Impact Stories in pilot until the submission-to-review lifecycle could be tested with real content. |
| 11 | What was the trade-off? | I balanced making useful onboarding available sooner against the trust risk of broadly promoting an untested story lifecycle. |
| 12 | Tell me about challenging an engineering solution and proposing an alternative. | I challenged whether labels alone met the story-discovery need and proposed natural-language search, with implementation and retrieval-quality outcomes still unconfirmed. |
| 13 | What would make this a delivered technical result? | A release record or working demonstration, a named engineering owner, and task-success evidence would be needed before claiming the discovery proposal delivered impact. |
| 14 | Tell me about a stakeholder disagreement that changed your plan. | When a stakeholder challenged my assumed outreach deadline and fragmented product engagement, I revised timing and deferred the newsletter pending alignment. |
| 15 | Is this a full Disagree and Commit example? | It demonstrates accepting a challenge and aligning execution, but the record does not establish sustained dissent against a final decision. |
| 16 | Why does this show Sr. Principal TPM readiness, and what needs another example? | It offers evidence of enterprise program formation, strategic adaptation, and influence without authority, while deeper production delivery and financial impact require additional evidence. |
| 17 | How would you describe your role precisely? | I founded, architected, and owned the program’s strategy, KPIs, partnerships, and operating model without claiming implementation of every platform capability or local workflow. |
| 18 | Why did you propose changing the FY27 adoption model after a successful FY26? | As tools matured, I shifted the strategy toward locally owned workflows and measurable value, while the uploaded document still describes the Ambassador layer as proposed. |
| 19 | Was the FY27 shift a reversal of FY26? | It was an evolution from readiness and peer learning toward accountable workflow execution as tools and organizational readiness improved. |
| 20 | What KPIs did you define? | I defined staged KPIs for membership and engagement, Champion coverage in organizations above 600 employees, and AI penetration in high-value workflows, with pilot productivity measured separately. |
| 21 | How did you identify high-value workflows? | I worked with business Champions to identify the activities consuming approximately 80% of their time and organized enablement and solution support around those priorities. |
| 22 | Who owned solutions after central enablement? | The lines of business retained solution ownership, while I coordinated AI SWAT enablement, expert support, and recurring platform-blocker escalation. |
| 23 | What did you personally build for Happy Oncall? | I prototyped a Codex-based assistant using local APIs, local MCP, and browser access to gather context for triage and handover reporting. |
| 24 | Why prioritize triage before other features? | I prioritized triage based on where on-call time was spent, then handover reporting that reused captured history, with knowledge-base and runbook generation deferred until context improved. |
| 25 | How did you measure the approximately 20% improvement? | Before-and-after comparisons of similar issues across two teams indicated approximately 20% effort savings, with sample size, observation window, and quality controls still to be established. |
| 26 | Is effort saved the same as MTTR improvement? | No; the established pilot claim concerns effort, and it cannot be relabeled as a reduction in mean time to resolution. |
| 27 | Why move from local access to remote connectors? | Local access enabled rapid prototyping, but setup overhead created scaling friction that motivated a remote connector. |
| 28 | How did you influence connector prioritization? | I combined community demand, votes, organizational data, and a business case to advocate prioritizing the remote DevOps portal connector ahead of Figma. |
| 29 | How did you address UX’s competing priority? | I connected designers through Champions, helped them successfully use a local workaround, and continued following up on remote Figma access. |
| 30 | What commitment did you secure? | I secured the DevOps platform team’s QBR commitment to prioritize the on-call work in the following quarter and agreed to refine community requirements before engineering capacity became available. |
| 31 | What was delivered versus committed? | The local prototype and two-team pilot were completed, while the broader platform work was a next-quarter commitment with delivery and savings not yet established. |
| 32 | Can you claim AI Champions caused Oracle’s company-wide adoption? | The program supported Oracle’s AI adoption goal, but its causal share of company-wide adoption was not isolated. |
| 33 | What permissions and security controls did Happy Oncall use? | Local APIs, MCP, and browser access are established, but the precise authorization scope, credential handling, read/write boundaries, and approval controls remain evidence gaps. |
| 34 | How did you evaluate answer quality and reliability? | The current record establishes an effort comparison but does not yet establish a formal accuracy, hallucination, reliability, or regression-evaluation protocol. |
| 35 | Who owned long-term production operations? | Lines of business retained solution ownership and a DevOps platform team committed roadmap capacity, but detailed production support, service levels, and maintenance responsibilities remain unconfirmed. |
| 36 | What would you improve? | I would establish workflow baselines, accountable local owners, capacity expectations, and outcome-validation gates earlier so adoption could be connected more credibly to business value. |

## Evidence boundaries and unresolved discrepancies

- Membership: the approved introduction uses the user’s self-reported 50-to-850 fiscal-year-end account; the uploaded PDF reports 702 in May 2026 and about 900 on a later homepage, alongside different kickoff counts, so dates and population definitions must be reconciled before treating these as equivalent figures.
- Coverage: the user reports achieved Champion representation in every organization above 600 employees; the PDF describes a proposed FY27 Ambassador cohort of 64 L3 organizations with at least 600 employees, so distinguish Champion versus Ambassador roles, achieved versus proposed status, date, and the exact employee threshold.
- Happy Oncall: retain the user’s two-team, approximately 20% effort-savings observation; four pilots or 30% MTTR, if encountered elsewhere, must be reconciled rather than merged into this claim.
- Enterprise adoption: the PDF records a later owner-confirmed 80% enterprise adoption milestone; it is not a demonstrated causal outcome of this program or an FY26 readiness metric.
- Measurement: pilot sample size, timing method, observation period, issue comparability, rework, output quality, and cost are not established here.
- Technical controls: precise architecture, permissions, credential handling, failure behavior, and evaluation remain open; do not borrow controls from the separate agentic TPM story.
- Durability: a QBR commitment is not production delivery; long-term production ownership and service levels still need confirmation.

## Sources used

- AI-Champions-Executive-Introduction.md, approved version read for this update.
- Use Case_AI Champions_20261016.pdf, including its nine preparation questions and nine follow-ups.
- User’s explicit AI Champions and Happy Oncall clarifications in this thread.
